HM-02.c01: Visible warnings are the markings and labels on packages and the **placards** on the truck; placards tell police and firefighters what you carry from a distance.
Most placard questions come down to two tables and one number: **1,001 pounds**.
**Marking** = required words and numbers on a package, such as the name, ID number, instructions, weight or UN marks.
**Bulk packaging** = a single container with a capacity greater than **119 gallons**; smaller containers are nonbulk.
**Residue** = the small amount of HazMat left in a package or tank after it is emptied; **gross weight** = packaging plus contents.
HM-02.c02: The most important marking is the **name of the HazMat**, the same name as on the shipping paper.
When required, the package shows the shipper or consignee name and address, shipping name and **ID number**, and required labels, plus words like RQ or HOT.
Packages with liquid containers inside have **orientation arrows** pointing upright.
Labels always match the **hazard class**; 2 or more labels go close together, next to the proper shipping name.
Compare the shipping paper with the markings and labels; if you don't know the material, **ask the shipper to contact your office**.
HM-02.c03: First read the shipping paper: look for a shipping name, hazard class and **ID number**, or a highlighted entry or **"X" or "RQ"** in the HM column.
Other clues: the shipper's business, such as paint, chemical or scientific supply, pest control or farm supply, or explosives and fireworks dealers.
**Cylinders and drums** often hold HazMat; also watch for tanks with diamond labels or placards, labels on packages, and handling precautions.
HM-02.c04: Hauling hazardous waste, you must **sign by hand** and carry a **Uniform Hazardous Waste Manifest**, and treat it as a shipping paper.
It shows the name and **EPA registration number** of shippers, carriers and destination; the shipper and **each carrier** sign it by hand.
Hand the waste **only** to another **registered carrier** or a disposal/treatment facility.
Keep your copy with all signatures and dates; the shipper writes **WASTE** before the shipping name and keeps the papers **3 years**.
HM-02.c05: **Placard before you drive**; an improperly placarded vehicle may move only in an **emergency** to protect life or property.
Use at least **4 identical** placards on both sides and both ends, each at least **9.84 in (250 mm)** square on point; the front one may go on tractor or trailer.
Each placard: easily seen, level and read left to right, at least **3 inches** from other markings, clear of attachments, clean, on a contrasting background.
Slogans such as "Drive Safely" are **not allowed** on placards.
To choose placards you need **3 facts**: hazard class, amount shipped, and total weight of all HazMat classes on the vehicle.
HM-02.c06: **Table 1** materials must be placarded whenever **any amount** is carried.
Table 1 includes explosives **1.1, 1.2 and 1.3**, 2.3 poison gas, 4.3 dangerous when wet, and 5.2 Type B temperature-controlled organic peroxide.
Table 1 also includes **6.1 inhalation hazard zone A and B** only, and 7 radioactive with a **Yellow III** label only.
HM-02.c07: Table 2 classes need placards only at **1,001 lb or more**, **counting the package** and adding all shipping papers (not for bulk packaging).
Example: 600 lb of Class 3 + 500 lb of Class 8 = **1,100 lb**, so placards are required; 900 lb alone in non-bulk packages needs none.
**No placard** for 6.2 infectious substances or ORM-D; the Class 9 placard is **not required** for domestic transportation.
**DANGEROUS** placards are optional for 1,001 lb or more of 2 or more Table 2 classes that need different placards.
DANGEROUS is not allowed for a class with **2,205 lb or more** loaded at one place; use its specific placard. Cargo or portable tanks may show FLAMMABLE for combustible.
HM-02.c08: **INHALATION HAZARD** → POISON GAS or POISON INHALATION placards plus class placards; the 1,000-pound exception does **not** apply.
A secondary hazard of dangerous when wet → **DANGEROUS WHEN WET** placard plus class placards, in any amount.
The hazard class or division number goes in the placard's **lower corner**.
You **may** show placards that aren't required, as long as they correctly identify the hazard of the material.
HM-02.c09: **Bulk packaging** = a single container with a capacity **greater than 119 gallons**.
A bulk package, and the vehicle carrying it, must be placarded **even if it holds only residue**, since a small amount left is still HazMat.
Most bulk packages are placarded on **all 4 sides**; certain ones need only 2 opposite sides or may show labels.
The **1,001-pound** Table 2 rule does **not** apply to bulk packaging.
